patient.chief_complaint: Grade 2-3 hepatic encephalopathy — constipation + opioid use as dual precipitants
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C. is a 64-year-old Asian man with hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 22) awaiting DAA therapy who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for progressive confusion and memory difficulty over 72 hours. The wife reports he has been increasingly confused since three days ago. He has not had a bowel movement in 5 days and has been in abdominal pain from severe constipation. The wife reveals that she gave him extra codeine phosphate 30 mg doses — up to 4 doses per day over the past 3 days — for his abdominal pain from constipation. He is prescribed codeine PRN but the wife was unaware it was contraindicated in cirrhosis. Codeine (an opioid) has two deleterious effects in cirrhotic patients: (1) it directly suppresses the central nervous system (hepatic impairment causes opioid accumulation due to reduced hepatic first-pass metabolism — standard doses cause supratherapeutic plasma levels); (2) it causes or worsens constipation, increasing colonic transit time and allowing more ammonia to be absorbed. The constipation itself is an independent HE precipitant — prolonged colonic transit allows gut bacteria more time to generate ammonia from nitrogenous substrates. The ammonia on admission is 164 µmol/L, confirming the dual-precipitant mechanism. EEG shows classic triphasic waves. The absence of fever and normal WBC argues against infectious precipitant. The urine drug screen is positive for codeine/opiates.

findings.description: Low-dose naloxone 0.04 mg IV administered. Partial improvement in alertness — eyes open to voice (GCS improves by 1-2 points) within 2 minutes. Speech slightly clearer. No complete normalization of consciousness.

output.result: Partial opioid reversal confirming opioid contribution to encephalopathy. Incomplete reversal indicates HE (ammonia) is the predominant mechanism — not pure opioid intoxication.
output.impression: Opioid (codeine) is a contributing precipitant — partial naloxone response confirms opioid effect. Ammonia 164 is the primary driver. STOP codeine permanently — opioids are CONTRAINDICATED in cirrhosis. Use safer analgesics (acetaminophen 2g/day maximum in stable cirrhosis, tramadol with caution). Continue lactulose + rifaximin as primary HE treatment.
recommendations: STOP codeine — contraindicated in hepatic impairment
AVOID all opioids in cirrhotic patients when possible
Safe analgesics in cirrhosis: acetaminophen ≤2g/day (NOT NSAIDs — nephrotoxic in cirrhosis)
Treat constipation with lactulose to prevent recurrence
Educate patient and family about opioid dangers in liver disease

output.query: Direct-acting antiviral therapy in hepatitis C cirrhosis — effect on hepatic encephalopathy

results.title: SVR with direct-acting antivirals in HCV cirrhosis reduces hepatic encephalopathy recurrence
results.finding: Achieving SVR12 with DAA therapy in compensated and decompensated HCV cirrhosis significantly reduces HE recurrence, improves MELD score (approximately 2-4 points reduction), and reduces liver-related mortality. AASLD/IDSA guidelines recommend DAA therapy in all patients with HCV cirrhosis regardless of decompensation status. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (8 weeks) or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (12 weeks) are preferred pan-genotypic regimens for decompensated cirrhosis.
results.relevance: High — initiate DAA after HE stabilization (decompensated cirrhosis may have drug-related hepatotoxicity risk — use Child-Pugh-appropriate regimen; avoid ribavirin in Child-Pugh C)

output.summary: HCV eradication with DAA therapy improves liver function and reduces HE recurrence. Urgently refer to hepatology for DAA initiation after HE stabilization. Preferred regimen for genotype 1a with decompensated cirrhosis: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 12 weeks (avoid ribavirin in Child-Pugh C — hemolytic anemia risk).

critical_actions: STOP codeine immediately — opioids accumulate in cirrhosis (reduced CYP2D6 and hepatic first-pass metabolism) and are contraindicated
Increase lactulose dose to treat constipation — constipation is an independent HE precipitant; titrate to 2-3 stools/day
Diagnostic paracentesis — exclude SBP even with clear constipation/opioid precipitant
DAA therapy referral — HCV eradication reduces HE recurrence and improves MELD
Educate family — codeine and other opioids are contraindicated in cirrhosis
Transplant evaluation — MELD-Na 22 + two overt HE episodes
contraindicated_actions: Continue or restart opioids (codeine, morphine, oxycodone) for pain management: Opioids are contraindicated in cirrhosis — hepatic impairment causes drug accumulation (reduced first-pass metabolism); all opioids worsen hepatic encephalopathy and increase mortality

Use NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) as opioid alternative in cirrhosis: NSAIDs are also contraindicated in cirrhosis — nephrotoxic via prostaglandin inhibition, worsen portal hypertension; use acetaminophen ≤2g/day instead
Defer lactulose because patient already on lactulose prophylaxis: Constipation indicates underdosing — increase lactulose dose until 2-3 stools/day achieved
Administer naloxone as full treatment without addressing HE: Opioid reversal alone does not treat hyperammonemia — ammonia-reducing therapy (lactulose/rifaximin) is the primary treatment
teaching_pearls: Codeine (and all opioids) are contraindicated in cirrhosis — reduced hepatic metabolism causes drug accumulation; always review the medication list for opioids when a cirrhotic presents with encephalopathy

Constipation is an underestimated HE precipitant — prolonged bowel transit time = more bacterial ammonia generation. Lactulose must be titrated to effect (2-3 stools/day), not given at arbitrary fixed doses
Partial naloxone reversal (not complete) distinguishes opioid-exacerbated HE from pure opioid intoxication — useful diagnostic test when urine opiates are positive
Safe pain management in cirrhosis: acetaminophen ≤2g/day (NOT NSAIDs, NOT opioids); tramadol with extreme caution at lowest effective dose
HCV eradication with DAAs in cirrhosis prevents HE recurrence — DAA therapy initiation after stabilization is a key management step
key_reasoning_points: Codeine in cirrhosis is a classic teaching error — patients with hepatic impairment have reduced hepatic CYP2D6 first-pass metabolism, causing codeine (and its active metabolite morphine) to accumulate to supratherapeutic plasma levels at standard doses

Constipation is the most frequently overlooked HE precipitant — prolonged colonic transit time allows urease-producing gut bacteria to generate more ammonia from dietary protein substrates; lactulose treats both constipation and HE

Partial naloxone reversal is the key diagnostic finding — full normalization of consciousness with naloxone suggests pure opioid intoxication; partial reversal with residual encephalopathy confirms dual-mechanism (opioid + HE)
Active HCV viremia (1.24 million IU/mL) contributes to ongoing hepatic inflammation and progressive cirrhosis — DAA therapy after stabilization is urgent; SVR12 reduces HE recurrence risk

NSAIDs are as dangerous as opioids in cirrhosis — prostaglandin inhibition reduces renal perfusion causing acute kidney injury and worsen portal hypertension; acetaminophen ≤2g/day is the safe analgesic in cirrhosis

metadata.primary_teaching_point: Constipation + codeine as dual HE precipitants; opioids contraindicated in cirrhosis; partial naloxone reversal; HCV DAA therapy reduces HE recurrence
